passages.title: Stoicism
content: 📌 Stoicism
Its continuing relevance comes partly from the [ _____ ] nature of its ideas.
Ancient Stoics
The philosophy began in Greece more than two thousand years ago.Its leading figures are well known even though their work was not produced for [ _____ ].
Stoic principles

A virtuous life was considered the route to happiness.People should learn to govern damaging emotions.Epictetus distinguished uncontrollable circumstances from the [ _____ ] that remain up to us.A Stoic interprets situations differently from people who regard them as [ _____ ].
The influence of Stoicism

George Washington arranged a [ _____ ] about Cato to encourage his soldiers.The French painter Delacroix followed Stoic teaching.Stoicism helped shape Adam Smith's thinking about [ _____ ].Several modern political leaders have drawn inspiration from ancient Stoic writing.
Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT)
This Stoic-influenced treatment is commonly used for [ _____ ].It teaches people to challenge irrational beliefs by relying on [ _____ ].
Business
Stoicism encourages people to view a difficulty as an [ _____ ].
Relevance of Stoicism
Following Stoic principles successfully requires sustained [ _____ ].It places strength of character above external rewards.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about Stoicism and its influence from the ancient world to the present. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions, 31 to 40. Ancient philosophy is sometimes treated as a matter of debates, lectures, and difficult books.

[00:58] AUDIO: Yet across history, people have also used it as a guide for dealing with problems and achieving remarkable things. The clearest example is Stoicism. Of all the ancient schools, it may be the most useful in everyday life, and that practical quality is a major reason people still find it attractive. It began in Greece more than two millennia ago, when Zeno of Citium founded it early in the 3rd century BC.

[01:30] AUDIO: Later followers included Epictetus, Cato, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius. Their ideas are remarkably familiar today, although the best-known Stoics did not write for publication. Cato wrote nothing for public release. Marcus Aurelius kept meditations as private reflections.

[01:55] AUDIO: Seneca was addressing letters, and what we know of Epictetus was recorded by one of his students. At the heart of Stoicism was the belief that lasting happiness could be gained through virtue. Reaching that statement meant learning to manage destructive feelings such as anger and jealousy instead of allowing them to govern us. Epictetus drew a clear distinction.

[02:22] AUDIO: Events outside us may be beyond our command, but the choices we make in responding to them remain within our control. The modern philosopher and writer Nassim Nicholas Taleb describes a Stoic as someone who changes their perspective on experiences that other people label negative. In his account, fear can become sensible caution, pain can bring personal change, mistakes can provide a beginning, and desire can be turned into purposeful action. This helps explain why Stoicism has influenced kings, presidents, artists, writers, and entrepreneurs across the centuries.

[03:07] AUDIO: The founders of the United States were among those influenced by Stoic thought. George Washington first encountered it through neighbors when he was 17. Years later, he arranged for a play about Cato to be performed in order to encourage his soldiers. Thomas Jefferson, meanwhile, kept a copy of Seneca beside his bed.

[03:32] AUDIO: Writers and artists were influenced, too. The celebrated French Romantic painter Eugène Delacroix, best known for liberty leading the people, was a committed Stoic, and even called the philosophy his source of consolation. Stoic teaching also reached economics. Adam Smith studied it at school under a teacher who had translated the work of Marcus Aurelius, and it later had a strong effect on his theories of capitalism.

[04:05] AUDIO: The same interest can be found among recent political leaders. Bill Clinton has said that he returns to Marcus Aurelius every year, while Barack Obama's calm approach to leadership has often been compared with Cato's. China's former premier Wen Jiabao described meditations as one of the two books he carried when traveling, and said he had read it more than a hundred times. Stoicism also shaped the work of Albert Ellis, who developed cognitive behavior therapy, or CBT.

[04:42] AUDIO: This approach helps people manage difficulties by altering unhelpful patterns of thought and behavior, and it is especially common in the treatment of depression. Patients are taught to question irrational beliefs that produce distorted thinking and to replace them with logic. In business, Stoicism has become increasingly popular because it can strengthen the resilience needed to recover from setbacks. Its followers are encouraged to reinterpret an obstacle as an opportunity, which is a valuable habit for any entrepreneur.

[05:21] AUDIO: I would say that Stoicism remains as useful now as it was two thousand years ago because it offers powerful guidance on living well. Take charge of what is within your control and accept what is not. Although simple to state, this principle demands considerable practice and may take a lifetime to master. For the Stoics, a good and happy life rested not on wealth, fame, power, or pleasure, but on a disciplined and principled character, an idea that still speaks to many people.
[06:01] AUDIO: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

passages.title: Copying Photos To Digital Format
content: 📌 Copying photos to digital format
Requirements
Standard photographs must measure between 4 cm and 30 cm.Each picture must be removed from its [ _____ ] and from any album.
Cost
Digitising 360 pictures costs £[ _____ ], including one disk.The finished package is dispatched after [ _____ ] has been received.
Services included in the price

Picture groups may be saved in separately named folders, such as [ _____ ].Staff can enhance the [ _____ ] and adjust the contrast when needed.Particularly delicate photographs are processed by [ _____ ].
Special restore service (costs extra)
An unwanted item may be deleted, or the [ _____ ] may be altered.Problems with [ _____ ] cannot be corrected.
Other information
The usual turnaround is [ _____ ] days.Use a cardboard container rather than one made of [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman asking an employee about a service that converts printed photographs into digital files. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 3. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 3.
[00:50] EMPLOYEE: Good morning, picture app. How can I help?
[00:53] WOMAN: Hello. I noticed your advert about transferring photographs onto a disk and I was hoping you could explain the service.
[01:02] EMPLOYEE: Of course. What would you like to ask?
[01:05] WOMAN: I have a whole box of family pictures that has been stored in the attic for years. Some are probably 50 or 60 years old and I want them converted into digital files.
[01:18] EMPLOYEE: Yes, we can certainly do that.
[01:21] WOMAN: Great. They come in lots of different sizes. Do you have any limits?
[01:26] EMPLOYEE: For the standard service, a photograph can be no larger than 30 cm. At the other end of the scale, 4 cm is the smallest size our equipment can manage.
[01:39] WOMAN: That sounds fine. A few are still inside a frame. Should I remove them before posting everything?
[01:47] EMPLOYEE: Yes, please. We cannot copy a picture while it is framed. Each photograph must also be loose rather than attached to a page in an album.
[01:58] WOMAN: No problem. Could you tell me roughly what the job would cost? I think there are about 360 pictures altogether.
[02:08] EMPLOYEE: The basic package for between 300 and 400 photographs costs £195.
[02:16] WOMAN: Does that price cover the disk as well?
[02:19] EMPLOYEE: It includes one disk. Additional copies are available for £5 each.
[02:25] WOMAN: Good. Am I expected to pay when I send the pictures?
[02:30] EMPLOYEE: Not at that stage. We copy them first and confirm the total charge. Your completed parcel is dispatched as soon as we receive the payment.
[02:40] WOMAN: I see.
[02:43] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 4 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 4 to 10.
[03:30] EMPLOYEE: Is there anything else you would like to know about what we offer?
[03:34] WOMAN: Yes. I have already divided the pictures into broad subject groups. Can you preserve those groups when you digitise them?
[03:42] EMPLOYEE: Certainly. Each group can go into its own folder on the disk, and you are welcome to choose a title for every folder.
[03:52] WOMAN: For example, could I label one grandparents?
[03:55] EMPLOYEE: Yes, exactly.
[03:57] WOMAN: Apart from scanning them, do you make any improvements to the images?
[04:02] EMPLOYEE: We examine every picture as part of the standard package. Where necessary, we can improve the colour and adjust the contrast, which often makes a noticeable difference.
[04:15] WOMAN: Some of mine are rather delicate. Is there a risk of damaging them?
[04:20] EMPLOYEE: No. If a print seems especially fragile, we process it by hand. We understand that old family photographs are extremely valuable to their owners.
[04:32] WOMAN: That is reassuring.
[04:33] EMPLOYEE: We can also edit a picture if requested. For instance, we may be able to take out an unwanted object or alter the background.
[04:43] WOMAN: Really? I may use that service after I have checked the pictures. One more thing. Several photographs are not properly in focus.
[04:55] WOMAN: Are you able to correct that?
[04:57] EMPLOYEE: Unfortunately, that is one problem we cannot repair.
[05:01] WOMAN: All right.
[05:03] EMPLOYEE: Can I give you any other details?
[05:05] WOMAN: Yes. How long does the whole process normally take?
[05:09] EMPLOYEE: We aim to finish the copying within ten days.
[05:13] WOMAN: Fine. I will pack the photographs into a box and send them to you.
[05:18] EMPLOYEE: A sturdy cardboard box is the safest choice. Plastic containers sometimes crack while they are in the post.
[05:27] WOMAN: Understood. Thank you for your help. Goodbye.
[05:30] EMPLOYEE: Goodbye.
[05:35] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Dartfield House School
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Dartfield House School"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear the head teacher of Dartfield House School speaking to parents about changes at the school. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Good morning and thank you for joining us.

[00:53] AUDIO: I want to explain several developments at the school that will affect your children. Our buildings were put up at very different times. Some date from the 1970s while others are less than five years old and Dartfield House itself is more than a hundred years old. A businessman named Neville Richards commissioned it as a residence for his family but he died before the work was finished.

[01:22] AUDIO: The person who inherited it sold it to the local council which used the building as administrative offices. There was later a proposal to turn it into a visitor information centre but funding was unavailable. Instead, the house became the starting point for this school when it opened 40 years ago. As the population nearby has expanded, the school has grown too.

[01:51] AUDIO: I can now update you on the lower school campus which lies across the road from the main one. We have received permission to develop both pieces of land. The younger pupils will transfer to purpose-built accommodation on the main campus while the present lower school buildings will make way for a housing development. Construction of the new school facilities should begin in the next few months.

[02:20] AUDIO: A change that will happen sooner involves lunchtime catering. Our current canteen remains popular and is frequently filled to capacity so the food itself is certainly not the issue. The difficulty is that a single counter serves everyone. Long queues means some pupils have very little time to eat before afternoon classes begin.

[02:47] AUDIO: To solve this a new food hall will open next week with several separate counters. To keep things moving smoothly, please talk to your children each morning and help them choose the kind of meal they want before they arrive. They can then go directly to the appropriate counter. All the meals will be healthy and the online system for adding money to each child's lunch card will continue unchanged.

[03:18] AUDIO: You may also be wondering about the old canteen. Its tables and chairs will remain and pupils may use the room to eat either a meal collected from the food hall or a packed lunch brought from home. We may eventually use part of the space for storage but we will first monitor how many pupils continue to eat there. Before you hear the rest of the talk you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

[04:22] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Let me return to the individual counters in the food hall. Each one will sell side dishes, desserts and drinks in addition to its main courses. The first counter, World Adventures, will feature food from a different country every day.

[04:49] AUDIO: It might offer Chinese dishes on Monday and Lebanese dishes on Tuesday for example. The full schedule will be arranged a week ahead so pupils can see the choices for every day of that week. Street life will also have an international focus, presenting food from three cultures at any one time. Pupils will be invited to propose ideas for the menus.

[05:17] AUDIO: We might begin with Thai, Ethiopian and Mexican dishes then replace one of those with Jamaican food for a week or two. Speedy Italian is designed especially for pupils who avoid meat and fish. Every item served at that counter will be suitable for vegetarians although there will still be enough variety to keep the menu interesting. That covers the food hall so I will finish with our optional after school programme.

[05:49] AUDIO: Swimming lessons are already so popular that there is a waiting list and off-road cycling remains another established favourite. We also currently train pupils to operate the sound and lighting equipment in our performance centre. Two additions are planned. Acting sessions will begin in the centre where pupils can attend for enjoyment or prepare for an annual play.

[06:18] AUDIO: In addition, a former pupil has donated a fine grand piano allowing us to offer piano tuition here for the first time rather than sending learners to the local college. That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Assignment On Sleep And Dreams
content: 📌 Assignment plan
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two psychology students, Susie and Luke, discussing an assignment about sleep and dreams. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:51] SUSIE: So, Luke, our next psychology assignment has to focus on sleep and dreams.

[00:57] LUKE: Yes. I have just read an article explaining why so many dreams disappear from our minds shortly after we wake. Most of mine are not especially interesting, but the writer's argument was that remembering every dream could make us confuse imagined experiences with events that really happened. Forgetting them therefore acts as a kind of safeguard.
[01:23] LUKE: I had always thought the problem was simply that our memory had too little capacity for all that information.
[01:30] SUSIE: That was my assumption, too. What is your view of the claim that dreams can tell us what will happen in the future?
[01:39] LUKE: Belief in that idea appears in cultures all around the world.

[01:42] SUSIE: True, and many people can describe a dream that later seem to come true. But one explanation is that thousands of our dreams never match later events, and those are ignored or forgotten. We only notice the rare cases when something we see or do in real life brings an old dream back to mind.

[02:05] LUKE: Exactly, so the match is really down to chance. I also read about segmented sleep. According to the theory, people centuries ago would wake during the night, talk or have something to eat, and then return to bed. I decided to try it.
[02:22] SUSIE: What made you do that?
[02:24] LUKE: Apparently it can improve creativity, though I am not sure why. I stopped after a week because the routine simply did not suit my lifestyle.

[02:35] SUSIE: Young children often nap during the day, of course. Some students here carried out a study last term to discover the age when preschool children should stop. They spent a long time selecting an appropriate research method, but the data showed no clear pattern, so they could not reach a firm answer.

[02:56] LUKE: Right? We should think about our own assignment now. In the previous one, I found the final stage difficult, because we had to judge how successful our work had been and explain that judgment. I also had some trouble producing the action plan.
[03:16] SUSIE: Planning was fine for me, but I lost marks on that self-assessment stage as well. My biggest difficulty, though, was the statistical analysis.
[03:25] LUKE: I see.
[03:28] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[04:15] SUSIE: Shall we work through the plan for this assignment?
[04:18] LUKE: Good idea.
[04:19] SUSIE: We need to begin with a research question. How about this? Is there a relationship between the number of hours someone sleeps and the number of dreams they remember?
[04:30] LUKE: That works. Next, we have to select our participants. Would about 12 students be enough?
[04:38] SUSIE: Yes. Should we recruit other people from the psychology department?
[04:44] LUKE: I would rather choose a different subject area. What about history?
[04:49] SUSIE: History students might have some interesting dreams. We could also consider literature students.
[04:56] LUKE: I do not really know anyone studying literature.
[04:58] SUSIE: All right. We will drop that suggestion. Then we need to choose our methodology. Observation is one possibility, but it does not seem suitable here.
[05:11] LUKE: No, I think it has to be self-reporting. We could ask the participants to complete the questions online.
[05:19] SUSIE: Since they need to respond immediately after waking, while they are still half asleep, paper would probably be more practical.
[05:27] LUKE: Agreed. We must also consult the ethical guidelines for this kind of investigation.
[05:34] SUSIE: Yes, because the study involves humans, and research with people is governed by particular rules.
[05:40] LUKE: I checked those rules for an earlier assignment. One section deals with assessing risk, and another says that any unnecessary stress for participants must be kept to a minimum.
[05:53] SUSIE: Let us hope the study does not give them nightmares.
[05:57] LUKE: Quite.

[05:59] SUSIE: After collecting the data, we will analyze it and calculate the correlation between our two variables, sleep duration and the number of dreams. Then we can display the findings visually in a graph.
[06:13] LUKE: Right. The final step is to reflect on the research and evaluate it. That all seems fairly straightforward.
[06:21] SUSIE: Yes. So now let's…

passages.title: Health Benefits Of Dance
content: 📌 Health benefits of dance
Recent findings

Every type of dance triggers hormones connected with positive feelings.Taking part with other people improves mood more than dancing by oneself.In an experiment involving university students, dancing increased [ _____ ].For people with mental health conditions, dance might be prescribed as [ _____ ].
Benefits of dance for older people

People can participate even when their level of [ _____ ] is low.Gentle dancing can support heart health.Improved [ _____ ] makes falls and related injuries less likely.Remembering sequences trains the [ _____ ] to work more quickly.Participants can experience a broader improvement in well-being.People gain more [ _____ ] to remain active in everyday life.Group dancing can reduce the [ _____ ] often experienced in later life.
Benefits of Zumba
A forty-minute session uses approximately as many [ _____ ] as some demanding workouts.
Findings reported in the American Journal of Health Behavior
Women with [ _____ ] benefited from attending Zumba regularly.For the participants, continued attendance became a [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about the health benefits of dancing. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. People everywhere dance when they are celebrating or simply enjoying themselves.

[00:57] AUDIO: Moving in response to music is found in every culture. What researchers have only recently begun to recognize, however, is that dance does more than lift our mood. It can also have substantial benefits for our health. Like other kinds of physical activity, dancing releases hormones such as dopamine, which help us feel calm and happy.

[01:23] AUDIO: At the same time, it can lower levels of stress and anxiety. Dance is usually a social experience as well, and that interaction appears to add to the positive feelings it creates. One study compared two situations, people dancing alone at home while following a video, and people taking part together in a studio class. Those who danced with a group said that their mood improved while the participants who danced by themselves reported no comparable change.

[01:56] AUDIO: Researchers from the universities of York and Sheffield conducted another experiment with students. Each participant spent five minutes in a laboratory listening to music and chose one of three activities, sitting still, pedaling an exercise bike or dancing. Everyone completed thinking tasks both before and afterwards. On the later problem-solving exercises, the dancers demonstrated a much higher level of creativity.

[02:30] AUDIO: Dr. Lovat at the University of Hertfordshire has suggested another application. He believes doctors could prescribe dance as therapy for people with mental health difficulties, including depression. Dance is already known to encourage teenage girls to exercise, but it can be equally valuable for people in their 60s and older. A major advantage is its accessibility.

[02:57] AUDIO: Nearly anyone can join in, even when their level of fitness is quite low. It is particularly useful for older adults who cannot or prefer not to run or complete demanding workouts. A study published in 2015 found that even gentle dancing supports a healthy heart. Other evidence shows that it can reduce falls and the resulting injuries, such as a broken hip, because regular practice improves balance.

[03:28] AUDIO: Some benefits are less obvious. Dance challenges the mind as well as the body, since participants must concentrate on remembering steps and sequences. This is valuable in later life because it trains the brain to process information more quickly and retain more of it. Current studies also indicate that older dancers experience an improved sense of well-being for as long as a week after a class.

[03:58] AUDIO: They often feel less tired and report greater motivation to remain active through everyday tasks, such as gardening or walking to local shops and parks. Ballroom and country dancing, which are both popular among older adults, take place in groups, partners cooperate, make physical contact and communicate on the dance floor. These experiences help people form new relationships and can ease the isolation that affects many older people. I also examined Zumba, an aerobic workout using Latin American dance movements.

[04:38] AUDIO: Around 15 million people in 180 countries now attend classes regularly. Professor John Porcari of the University of Wisconsin studied experienced female participants and found that a 40-minute class burns roughly 370 calories. That is comparable with fairly demanding activities such as step aerobics and kickboxing. Research published in the American Journal of Health Behavior followed women with obesity who attended Zumba three times a week for 16 weeks.

[05:17] AUDIO: On average, they lost 1.2 kilograms and reduced their body fat percentage by one point. More importantly, they enjoyed the sessions enough to make attendance a habit, continuing to go at least once a week. That level of commitment is unusual in an aerobic exercise program. Dance will not produce the same physical gains as a high-intensity workout, but it is likely to become even more popular because it offers such an enjoyable way to stay fit.
[05:55] AUDIO: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

content: 📌 Junior Cycle Camp

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a mother telephoning a children's cycling camp to ask about a course for her son. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
[00:49] JAKE: Junior Cycle Camp, Jake speaking. How can I help?
[00:53] WOMAN: Hello, I'm calling to find out more about the cycling camp because I'm considering sending my son.

[01:00] JAKE: Certainly, it runs every weekday morning during the summer holiday and the emphasis is on essential riding skills and staying safe. We offer eight levels starting with children age 3. How old is your son?
[01:17] WOMAN: Charlie's 7. He can ride already, but he still needs some practice before he'd be safe cycling on the road.

[01:25] JAKE: Level 5 would probably suit him. The children begin on our own site and eventually work towards riding on public roads. Before that though, we take them to the park where they can practice away from traffic.
[01:41] WOMAN: I see. Could you explain a little about the instructors?
[01:46] JAKE: Of course. Our staff wear different colors, so they're easy to identify. The three supervisors have red shirts. They assist the instructors and cover for me when necessary.
[01:59] JAKE: The instructors themselves wear blue shirts and each one is in charge of a class.
[02:05] WOMAN: Right.

[02:06] JAKE: Before we employ anyone as an instructor, they must provide a reference from somebody who has watched them work with children, perhaps while babysitting. After that, they complete our training which covers planning lessons and looking after the children properly. The standard is very high.
[02:28] WOMAN: Good. And how large would Charlie's class be?

[02:32] JAKE: We never have more than eight children in one class, so the instructor gets to know everyone well. Most of the morning is spent cycling, but there are quieter periods too. The instructor may tell a story linked to cycling or organize a game for the group. The children really enjoy it.
[02:53] WOMAN: It sounds great. Do you cancel the sessions when there's rain?
[02:58] JAKE: No, they still go ahead. Everyone puts on waterproof clothing and carries on riding.
[03:06] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions six to ten. Now listen and answer questions six to ten.
[03:52] WOMAN: Is there anything in particular that Charlie needs to bring?
[03:56] JAKE: Some spare clothes would be useful, especially in poor weather, and he should bring a snack for the break.
[04:04] WOMAN: Does he need to bring a drink as well?
[04:07] JAKE: No, we supply drinks, but please make sure he wears shoes rather than sandals.
[04:14] WOMAN: Of course. Charlie currently has to take medication every few hours, so I'll send that with him.
[04:21] JAKE: That's fine. Give us the schedule for it, and we'll make sure he takes it at the right times.
[04:27] WOMAN: Thank you.

[04:29] JAKE: There are also a few arrangements for the first day. Classes usually begin at 930, but that morning Charlie should arrive at 920. They still finish at 1230. We need those extra ten minutes, because several checks have to be done.

[04:48] JAKE: Most importantly, we'll check that every child's helmet fits correctly. If Charlie's doesn't, we'll adjust it or provide a different one, since he must wear it whenever he's on the bike.
[05:02] WOMAN: Naturally.
[05:03] JAKE: Once that's finished, the instructors will be ready to meet their groups in the tent. It's very easy to spot. Each instructor will then take the class away to begin.
[05:15] WOMAN: All right. How much is the camp for one week?
[05:18] JAKE: It's $199. That's only a little more than last year's fee of $190, and places are being taken quite quickly.
[05:29] WOMAN: In that case, I'd like to book a place for...
[05:35] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute

passages.title: Working In The Agriculture And Horticulture Sectors
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Working In The Agriculture And Horticulture Sectors"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a recruitment consultant talking about careers in agriculture and horticulture. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Good morning everyone, I'm Megan Baker and I work as a recruitment consultant for AVT Recruitment Specialists.

[00:59] AUDIO: Our agency concentrates on jobs in agriculture and horticulture. That includes areas such as producing fresh food and maintaining gardens and public parks. These fields can offer some distinctive career benefits. To begin with, many roles suit people who don't want a rigid 40-hour schedule and need to arrange work around commitments, such as looking after children.

[01:30] AUDIO: That flexibility matters to a large number of candidates. Some enjoy the possibility of working in the countryside among plants and trees rather than buildings. Although this isn't something every post can offer, there can also be clear health advantages, particularly when the work keeps you moving instead of sitting in front of a computer all day. Pay is attractive in certain roles, but it varies considerably.

[02:03] AUDIO: Some positions may also involve travelling abroad, depending on the job, though that doesn't appeal to everybody. Naturally, outdoor employment brings a few difficulties. Summer can be pleasant, but cold, windy weather may make the work extremely uncomfortable. Certain jobs require reasonable fitness, although machinery has reduced that demand compared with the past.

[02:33] AUDIO: Workplace accidents have actually declined because health and safety standards are now much stricter. However, many posts are based in remote, quiet places, so they won't suit anyone who prefers the activity and company of a city. People sometimes worry about obtaining suitable housing too, but we generally find that this problem is resolved. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

[03:42] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. I'll now describe several interesting vacancies that are currently available through our agency. The first is for a fresh food commercial manager with a major producer that supplies several leading supermarkets. The business moves very quickly and operates on narrow profit margins.

[04:11] AUDIO: Employees work intensively, but they also enjoy themselves together, so the position would suit somebody sociable. Another opening is for an agronomist who will advise farmers about crop nutrition, pest control and recent legislation affecting agricultural practice. A candidate with the right qualities could progress rapidly within the organisation. Applicants must, however, already have extensive knowledge of the farming sector.

[04:47] AUDIO: A large supermarket also needs a fresh produce buyer for a 12-month contract covering maternity leave. The successful applicant must have experience of administration, planning and purchasing fresh produce. In return, the salary is highly competitive. We have also been asked to find a sales manager for a group of garden centres.

[05:15] AUDIO: The manager will travel to different centres across the region to check that excellent customer service is being maintained. The role is only appropriate for somebody willing to live locally. There is a further vacancy for a tree technician involving tree cutting, forestry and conservation duties. Candidates need a clean driving licence and safety training.

[05:44] AUDIO: A year's practical experience is preferred, although the employer may consider somebody who has only recently finished a suitable training programme. Finally, a farm worker is required for varied duties, including sowing and harvesting crops, maintaining machinery and caring for animals. One benefit is the possibility of renting a small cottage on the estate, as well as receiving a competitive salary. A driving licence and experience of operating a tractor are both essential.
[06:26] AUDIO: That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answer.

passages.title: Experiment On Artificial Sweeteners
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Experiment On Artificial Sweeteners"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, Adam and Rosie, planning a presentation about diet and obesity. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:52] ADAM: Right, Rosie, shall we start pulling together some ideas for our presentation on diet and obesity?
[00:58] ROSIE: Yes, let's.
[00:59] ADAM: I could cover the experiment I carried out on whether people can distinguish ordinary sugar from artificial sweeteners.
[01:07] ROSIE: Was that the one where you served drinks containing one or the other and asked everyone to identify which they had?

[01:14] ADAM: That's right. Working out the procedure took a long time, especially because the participants couldn't be allowed to know which drink they received. There were so many volunteers that recording exactly what each person had was difficult as well.
[01:31] ROSIE: And were they generally able to recognize the difference?
[01:36] ADAM: Surprisingly, yes. I'd expected most of them not to manage it, but the majority did.
[01:43] ROSIE: Then I could discuss my experiment on the amount of fat in nuts and whether the figure printed on the packet was reliable.
[01:51] ADAM: You crushed the nuts and added a chemical that took up the fat, didn't you?

[01:57] ROSIE: Yes. The result was troublesome because I measured far less fat than the packet stated, though I'm confident the manufacturer's figure was correct. I probably left the nuts too coarse, and the scales may not have been precise enough either. I'd like to repeat it one day.
[02:18] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.

[03:03] ADAM: So, what could we say about ways to help people lose weight? Restaurants have several possibilities. I read that diners tend to select dishes shown first or last on a menu more often than those in the middle. If the lower calorie choices occupied those positions, customers might choose them without consciously noticing why.
[03:28] ROSIE: Food producers could surely do more to promote healthier eating as well.
[03:33] ADAM: In what way?

[03:34] ROSIE: The calorie information on labels can be extremely difficult to interpret, and I suspect manufacturers sometimes make it that way deliberately. High calorie food often tastes better, which helps them sell more of it.
[03:50] ADAM: Exactly. A pizza label might state the calories for only one quarter, making the number look reasonable, even though very few people stop after a quarter.
[04:01] ROSIE: That's true.
[04:02] ADAM: Another possibility is encouraging everyone to be more physically active.

[04:07] ROSIE: Yes. The English guidance is at least 30 minutes of brisk walking on five days each week. Around 40% of men and 30% of women claim they achieve that. Yet motion sensors show the real figures are only 6% for men and 4% for women.
[04:29] ADAM: That difference helps explain the rise in obesity.
[04:33] ROSIE: But how do you persuade people to exercise more?

[04:35] ADAM: Consider a railway station. Travelers are more likely to use stairs if they reach them before the escalator, and a broader staircase lets more people take it simultaneously. Small alterations to the surroundings can shape behavior without people being aware of it.
[04:54] ROSIE: And even if the effect is modest, repeating it every day makes it significant.
[05:00] ADAM: True. Still, I'm beginning to wonder whether exercise belongs in our presentation at all.
[05:08] ROSIE: We've already read a fair amount about it, though.
[05:11] ADAM: We have, but including it would make the topic too broad. Our tutor specifically asked us to concentrate on nutritional causes and solutions.
[05:21] ROSIE: You're right. We already have plenty of material on that, and keeping to it will make the presentation more manageable.
[05:30] ADAM: What should we tackle now, then? Our next lecture doesn't start for another half hour.
[05:35] ROSIE: Let's choose the material we're going to use and decide its sequence. Once that's settled, we can work out which slides to prepare.
[05:44] ADAM: Fine, let's do that.
[05:48] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to...

content: 📌 Hand knitting
Renewed interest in knitting

Very old garments show that knitting was practised internationally.A familiar image is a [ _____ ] sitting beside the fire.A [ _____ ] ago, the craft was expected to die out.More people are enrolling in knitting classes.Sales of knitting [ _____ ] are increasing as well.
Advantages of knitting
can help families facing [ _____ ] problemsrequires only [ _____ ] abilities and little initial expenseprovides relief from the pressures of modern life
Origins and early practice

The date when knitting began is unknown.The earliest surviving garments were generally [ _____ ] rather than flat.The first needles were made from materials including wood and [ _____ ].Early yarn often felt [ _____ ] against the skin.The spinning wheel helped wool become the leading yarn.Each region developed a characteristic [ _____ ].People knitted during duties such as watching over [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about the history and present-day value of hand knitting. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Good morning.

[00:52] AUDIO: Today we're going to examine hand knitting, an important form of creative work. Ancient knitted clothing has been discovered in many different countries, which shows that the craft has a long, worldwide history. When knitting is mentioned, many of us visualise an elderly relative, perhaps a grandmother, sitting beside the fire and making clothes for the family. That comfortable domestic picture can make the craft seem old-fashioned.

[01:27] AUDIO: In fact, only a decade ago, people were predicting that knitting would disappear from ordinary life. Humans had made their own clothes for centuries, but skills like this declined once industrial machinery took over, largely because they stopped being handed down within families. That trend is now reversing. Enrolment in knitting classes is growing in many countries as people look for proper instruction.

[02:01] AUDIO: And sales of knitting equipment are rising too. Why then learn to knit when machines can produce clothes so easily? One reason is that the craft still offers practical advantages. In the past, many people knitted because ready-made clothing was unaffordable, and it can still help anyone dealing with economic hardship.

[02:28] AUDIO: A household with several children needing warm winter clothes may save a considerable amount. Making the garments yourself can also be satisfying, even though the skills needed at the beginning are basic and the initial cost is very small. For people today, however, the greater benefits concern well-being. We may spend as much as nine hours a day online, so creating something with our hands can be particularly rewarding.

[03:03] AUDIO: It provides a welcome release from the pressure of a fast, technology-driven life. Let's now go back to the beginnings of the craft. Nobody knows exactly when knitting started, although archaeological discoveries give us a good deal of evidence to consider. One striking feature of the earliest clothing is that most pieces were round rather than flat.

[03:33] AUDIO: Finds from 3rd and 4th century Egypt include socks and gloves made in a single piece with four or five needles, unlike many modern patterns that use only two. The first needles were carved by hand from wood and other natural substances such as bone. Modern versions, by contrast, are generally steel or plastic and produce the familiar clicking noise. Early knitters used linen, hemp, cotton and wool for their yarn, and these fibres were often rough against the skin.

[04:14] AUDIO: Later, the spinning wheel made it possible to create finer yarn in much larger quantities, helping wool become dominant, partly because of its warmth. Since knitting was practised for many purposes across so many places, each region gradually developed its own style. These visual differences allow researchers to connect fragments of knitted clothing with the wearer's home region or occupation. As I mentioned earlier, people in poorer communities could earn extra money from knitting while carrying out other duties.

[04:57] AUDIO: For centuries, men, women and children appear to have used every available moment – knitting while watching sheep, walking to market or travelling by boat. So, let's turn now to consider… That is the end of part four. You now have one minute.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a man asking the owner of a holiday cottage about renting accommodation. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:52] SHIRLEY: Hello, Shirley Fitzgerald speaking.
[00:55] TOM: Hello. I was trying to reach Jack Fitzgerald because I'm interested in hiring one of your cottages.
[01:03] SHIRLEY: I'm Shirley, Jack's wife. We run the cottages jointly so I can deal with your inquiry.
[01:11] TOM: That's good. I'm Tom. Friends stayed in Granary Cottage last year and recommended it. My wife and I would like a week there in May.
[01:22] SHIRLEY: Which week were you considering?
[01:25] TOM: Ideally the one starting on the 14th.
[01:28] SHIRLEY: Let me look. Unfortunately, somebody has already taken it then. It is available for seven nights from the 28th, and that is its only free week in May.
[01:41] TOM: We might be able to rearrange things. What is the weekly price?
[01:46] SHIRLEY: As that date falls at the start of the high season, the charge is 550 pounds.
[01:52] TOM: That is rather above our limit. We had allowed no more than 500 pounds for the accommodation.
[02:02] SHIRLEY: In that case, there may be another possibility. We have just turned a different building into a cottage and named it Cherville Cottage.
[02:10] TOM: Could you repeat the name?
[02:13] SHIRLEY: Cherville C-H-E-R-V for Victor I-L.
[02:20] TOM: Right. The herb.
[02:23] SHIRLEY: Exactly. It grows wild locally. That cottage is available for your preferred week and the rent is 480 pounds.
[02:32] TOM: Could you describe it for me?
[02:35] SHIRLEY: Certainly. The structure was originally a garage. It is slightly smaller than Granary Cottage.
[02:43] TOM: Does it also accommodate two people?
[02:46] SHIRLEY: Yes. It has one double bedroom.
[02:50] TOM: Is there any outside space?
[02:53] SHIRLEY: There is a garden reached through French doors from the living room. We supply two deck chairs as well. A patio is planned, although I cannot promise it will be ready before May.
[03:05] TOM: That's fine.
[03:06] SHIRLEY: The entrance faces the former farmyard. There is plenty of space at the front for parking, along with several trees and plants in pots.
[03:19] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten. Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.
[04:02] TOM: And what equipment does the cottage have? I assume there are ordinary things such as a cooker and a fridge.
[04:14] SHIRLEY: The kitchen area contains a fridge freezer, and we have recently installed an electric cooker.
[04:21] TOM: Is a washing machine provided?

[04:24] SHIRLEY: Yes. The living room also has a television which can play DVDs. There was not enough room in the bathroom for a bath, so we fitted a shower instead. Many guests prefer one now, in any case.
[04:41] TOM: It uses less water, unless someone stays under it all day.
[04:47] SHIRLEY: Quite.
[04:48] TOM: How is the place heated? Even in May, the weather can turn chilly.

[04:54] SHIRLEY: It has central heating, as well as a stove if you would like a fire. We supply as much wood as you need. It has a much pleasanter smell than coal, and makes the room feel very comfortable. We use the same kind of stove at home.
[05:11] TOM: That sounds lovely. Perhaps winter would be the best time to appreciate it.

[05:18] SHIRLEY: Once our fire is lit, we rarely feel like going anywhere. I should also mention the views. From the living room you can see a well-known old stone bridge, one of the earliest in this area, quite close to the cottage. The bedroom faces the other way, towards the hills and the monument on the summit.
[05:40] TOM: Everything sounds ideal. I'd like to reserve it. Do you require a deposit?
[05:48] SHIRLEY: Yes. To confirm the booking, we take 30%, which comes to 144 pounds.
[05:56] TOM: When is the remaining amount due?
[05:59] SHIRLEY: Since your stay is in May, please pay it by the final day of March.
[06:04] TOM: Fine.
[06:06] SHIRLEY: Excellent. I'll just need to take down your details.
[06:12] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute.

passages.title: Local Council Report On Traffic And Highways
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Local Council Report On Traffic And Highways"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a local council meeting about transport issues and planned changes to a recreation ground. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. We'll move on to the next item, which concerns traffic and highways, Councillor Thornton.

[00:56] AUDIO: Thank you. Well, we've received the findings from last month's survey on traffic and road transport in the town. Most respondents were content with the condition of the roads, a small number mentioned potholes, and those will be dealt with. However, the strongest concern was the growing number of heavy vehicles taking our local roads in order to avoid congestion elsewhere.

[01:25] AUDIO: We had anticipated more criticism from commuters about the reduced train service, but that appears to have caused relatively little difficulty. The riverside cycle path has attracted plenty of cyclists and walkers since it was resurfaced last year. Passing other users can be awkward though, so an extra strip will shortly be added along one edge to widen it. In the longer term, we hope to extend the route right across the town, but that work is not planned for the near future.

[02:03] AUDIO: Unfortunately, the proposed pedestrian crossing beside the post office has been delayed. Money had already been allocated for the current financial year. There were then reports that the post office might relocate, in which case the crossing would not have been needed. It has now confirmed that it will remain in place.

[02:27] AUDIO: The problem is that the highways department regards our intended site as unsafe because it lies close to a bend. We will therefore have to reconsider the location. On Station Road, drivers sometimes wait for quite a while when the level crossing is closed. New notices ask them to switch their engines off during these delays, so pedestrians on the pavement are not exposed to exhaust fumes.

[02:58] AUDIO: Cyclists have also been fastening bikes to the railings outside the ticket office, but the station will solve that by installing cycle racks. Before you hear the remainder of the meeting, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Our next item is the proposed improvement of the recreation ground.

[04:02] AUDIO: Councillor Thornton will report again. Since the recreation ground was enlarged, we have consulted residents about making it both more useful and more appealing. Please look at the map on the screen. The river is along the northern boundary, while the community hall stands close to the entrance from the road.

[04:26] AUDIO: At present, cars park between the hall and the row of trees to its east. Because this creates a risk for people on foot, we propose putting the new car park on the other side of the community hall, immediately beside the building. The cricket pitch will also move. We have bought extra land on the eastern side of the ground, beyond the trees.

[04:52] AUDIO: The pitch is currently too close to the road, so it will be placed in that newly acquired area on the far side of the tree line. This should prevent stray balls from reaching vehicles or pedestrians. A children's playground is planned as well. A footpath will lead to it from the community hall, and it will occupy the area next to the river.

[05:19] AUDIO: We first considered a position near the road, but the riverside setting should be more pleasant. The skateboard ramp is used by children of several ages. Although moving it towards the river was discussed, the final decision is to put it in the southeast corner, close to the road. The pavilion serves both footballers and cricketers, and is already in a convenient position.

[05:49] AUDIO: It will remain where it is, to the west of the row of trees and near the river, within easy reach of both pitches. Finally, a new board for local notices will be installed. Anyone entering the recreation ground from the road will find it immediately on their right. That is the end of part two.
[06:14] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: City Bike-Sharing Schemes
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "City Bike-Sharing Schemes"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:01] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, Jake and Amy, discussing city bike-sharing schemes for a university report. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:54] JAKE: Now that we have gathered the case studies, we need to decide how to organize our report on urban bike-sharing.
[01:01] AMY: I agree. Let's begin with the main benefits. These schemes let people collect a bicycle near one part of a city and return it somewhere else, so they can use one without owning it.
[01:14] JAKE: That convenience matters, although the charges are not always low enough for regular users.
[01:21] AMY: True, but if some commuters cycle instead of driving, there are fewer cars competing for space. That can make a noticeable difference on crowded roads.
[01:33] JAKE: Yes, reducing traffic must be one of the strongest arguments for a scheme.
[01:39] AMY: And people who would otherwise sit in a car or on a bus get some exercise. Even short journeys can increase their daily activity.
[01:48] JAKE: I'd put that alongside the traffic benefit. It affects a large number of users and may continue for years.
[01:56] AMY: Cleaner air is another possible advantage, though the evidence is uneven because buses, delivery vans, and other vehicles still produce most of the emissions in some cities.
[02:09] JAKE: Right, so we should mention it, but not present it as one of the two most important benefits.
[02:16] AMY: What about our recommendations for making schemes successful?
[02:20] JAKE: Some operators spend a lot on sophisticated bicycles with satellite locators. They are useful if a bike disappears, but I don't think every bicycle has to have one.
[02:32] AMY: Nor do I. What people really need is an app that works properly. If booking or paying becomes complicated, they simply give up.
[02:41] JAKE: Absolutely. The software has to be straightforward as well as reliable.
[02:47] AMY: Several reports argue that a city should complete a huge network of protected routes before launching the bikes.
[02:55] JAKE: Good routes help, certainly. But a few schemes have attracted plenty of users before the network was finished. I wouldn't call that essential.
[03:05] AMY: And I see no reason to insist on a single operator. Two companies can compete successfully if their systems are compatible.
[03:14] JAKE: Agreed. The other essential point is communication. Residents need a clear campaign showing where the bikes are, how to hire them, and why the scheme is worthwhile.
[03:27] AMY: Yes. Without proper publicity, even a technically excellent system may be ignored.
[03:36] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[05:06] AMY: Shall we move on to the individual cities and summarize our opinions of their schemes?
[05:12] JAKE: Let's start with Amsterdam. Cycling was already part of everyday life there, and most residents seem to have their own bicycles.
[05:21] AMY: Which is why I didn't expect shared bikes to attract so many journeys.
[05:26] JAKE: Neither did I. The level of demand is remarkable given how many private bicycles there are.
[05:33] AMY: Dublin is interesting, too. I think visitors made the scheme popular because they wanted an easy way to get around the center.
[05:41] JAKE: I'm not convinced. Tourists use it. But I think low membership fees explain the success. The buses and trams already cover most central routes.
[05:52] AMY: So we disagree about the main reason in that case. What shall we say about London?
[05:58] JAKE: The system is dependable and well-maintained, but it has not reached enough outer districts.
[06:04] AMY: Exactly. More money needs to go into additional docking points and safer connections between them.
[06:12] JAKE: Buenos Aires gives us the opposite kind of example. The city added cycling routes, docking stations, and the payment system as one coordinated project.
[06:23] AMY: That careful planning is probably why large numbers of new cyclists began using it so quickly.
[06:31] JAKE: New York made a serious mistake with its initial charges. A short rental could cost more than another form of transport.
[06:39] AMY: We both thought that price would put many potential users off, however attractive the bicycles were.
[06:46] JAKE: Finally, Sydney. On paper it looked ideal. Pleasant weather in many months, a growing center, and plenty of tourists.
[06:56] AMY: Yet the number of journeys stayed low. I found the result disappointing.
[07:01] JAKE: So did I. It achieved far less than we expected, although perhaps later investment will improve it.
[07:09] AMY: Good. We have our examples. Let's now decide how much space each city should receive in the report and then divide the writing between us.
[07:22] NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

passages.title: The Extinction Of The Dodo Bird
content: 📌 The extinction of the dodo bird
The dodo was a large flightless bird that lived on the island of Mauritius.
History

1507 – Portuguese vessels carrying [ _____ ] called at Mauritius for supplies.1638 – the Dutch created a [ _____ ] on the island.The birds were hunted as a source of food.The last known dodo was killed in 1681.
Description

Written reports and artworks may not provide dependable evidence.One Dutch artwork makes the dodo appear extremely [ _____ ].The only preserved soft tissue still in existence is a [ _____ ].Study of the skeleton indicates that strong joints permitted rapid [ _____ ].Its small wings probably helped it maintain [ _____ ] on rough ground.Its [ _____ ] was of average size, not particularly small.A highly developed sense of [ _____ ] helped it locate food.
Reasons for extinction

Hunting is no longer regarded as the main explanation.Dogs and monkeys were deliberately introduced by sailors.[ _____ ] arrived unintentionally on ships and ate the birds’ eggs.Agriculture resulted in the destruction of the [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the dodo bird and the reasons for its extinction. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

[00:52] AUDIO: Today I'm going to examine one of the best-known examples of extinction, the dodo. The English expression, as dead as the dodo, is still used for something that has completely disappeared. Yet the bird lived successfully for a very long time on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean. It stood roughly a metre high and, although it could no longer fly, it survived among the trees that covered the island.

[01:26] AUDIO: Europeans first recorded the island in 1507, when Portuguese ships stopped there on their return journey to Europe. They were transporting spices and used Mauritius as a place to obtain fresh food and water. But they did not remain there. Permanent occupation began in 1638, when the Dutch established a settlement.

[01:55] AUDIO: The newcomers hunted dodos for meat, even though some sailors said the flavour was unpleasant. The last known bird was killed in 1681. Reconstructing the dodo's appearance is difficult. Sailors left written accounts and artists produced several pictures, but neither source is necessarily accurate.

[02:21] AUDIO: In the most familiar Dutch painting, the bird looks extremely fat. By contrast, an Indian artist working at about the same time showed a much slimmer animal, so the Dutch image may be misleading. People did try to preserve specimens, but no complete body remains. At the beginning of the 17th century, four dried pieces were recorded.

[02:49] AUDIO: Three were subsequently lost, leaving a head as the only surviving example of the bird's soft tissue. Various bones have been recovered too, although just one complete skeleton is known. That skeleton has recently been analysed, and the findings challenge several traditional ideas. Old descriptions called the dodo slow and awkward, whereas its powerful knee joints suggest it was capable of rapid movement.

[03:23] AUDIO: One early sailor even complained that the birds were difficult to catch. Its small wings could not lift it into the air, but probably helped it maintain balance on uneven ground. Examination of the skull also showed that its brain was average in size, rather than unusually small. Relative to the body, it resembled the brain of a pigeon, a bird recognised for its intelligence.

[03:54] AUDIO: Finally, the skull indicates a particularly developed sense of smell, which would have helped the dodo locate ripe fruit and other food in dense vegetation. These findings imply that the dodo was more capable of protecting itself than earlier accounts suggested. Nevertheless, it vanished less than two centuries after Europeans arrived. Hunting was once regarded as the explanation, but researchers now think several factors were involved.

[04:31] AUDIO: Sailors deliberately brought dogs, which could attack the birds, and monkeys, which competed for the fruit they ate. Ships also carried rats accidentally. They spread rapidly across the island and consumed dodo eggs. Because a female laid only one egg at a time, this would have caused serious damage to the population.

[04:57] AUDIO: Even so, the strongest explanation now concerns agriculture rather than hunting or introduced animals. The forest that once covered Mauritius provided the dodo's habitat. Settlers cut it down to create farmland and grow crops such as sugar. So the bird lost the environment on which it depended.
